items.title: Brewery closes Mississauga bar and restaurant, but beer brand will live on
items.summary: The music has stopped and the taps at Stonehooker Brewing Co. have gone quiet, but customers aren’t saying goodbye to the Mississauga brewery’s beer just yet. Stonehooker’s Biergarten CODA and its restaurant, bar and hospitality operation closed for good on Sept. 7, marking the end of the brewery’s run as a destination for pints, food, live music and events on Lakeshore Road East. But the Stonehooker beer store remains open and the brewery’s beer continues to be available at the LCBO. Owner Ross Noel says that’s an important distinction for customers who may have interpreted the closure as the end of Stonehooker altogether. com. “The brand has value. ” Stonehooker announced the closure last month, saying the brewery’s hospitality operation would be winding down. The final day brought one last celebration for customers who wanted to enjoy the space before it closed. Now, however, customers can still visit the location to purchase Stonehooker beer from the retail store. m. m. m.

items.summary: The incidents occurred early morning Thursday, Sept. m. Peel police are looking for a male suspect following a rash of vehicle break-ins in Mississauga. Police are looking for a man in connection with dozens of vehicle break-ins in Mississauga. m. Sept. 3. “The suspect unlawfully entered 32 vehicles in the area by smashing windows or accessing unlocked vehicles,” police said in Sept. 6 news release. “Multiple valuables were stolen. ” Police describe the suspect as white, about 30 years old, with a medium build. He was wearing a jacket with POLO written on the back collar, joggers and two-tone coloured shoes with a white sole and also had a backpack, police said in the news release, which contained a surveillance camera image of the suspect. items.title: Canadian dessert chain closes location in Mississauga
items.summary: A Canadian dessert chain has closed in Mississauga. BeaverTails and Shelly’s Chill at 213 Queen St. S. in Streetsville are marked as permanently closed on Google Maps, and customers reported the closure on social media. The BeaverTails location is no longer listed on the company website. Attempts to contact Shelly’s Chill was unsuccessful. BeaverTails are flat donuts topped with sweets such as chocolate hazelnut spread, maple spread, peanut butter, bananas, cheesecake spread, brownie pieces, crushed Oreo cookies or Reese’s Pieces. BeaverTails locations also have fries, poutine, hot dogs wrapped in a pastry, ice cream, lemonade and smoothies. The chain started as a wooden booth in the heart of Ottawa’s historic ByWard Market in 1980. It has since grown to about 50 shops in tourist towns and resort villages and over 150 mobile shops, according to the website. The Streetsville location opened in 2022, and Shelly’s Chill operated in the same space. Shelly’s Chill served chicken sandwiches, bowls, shakes and fries.

items.title: AI data centres again a topic of discussion in Mississauga
items.summary: Just over a month after imposing a moratorium on construction of huge AI data centres in Mississauga, city officials are poised to discuss the issue at length once again on Wednesday. A report from senior City of Mississauga staff outlining the Ontario government’s latest “playbook” for the building of such large facilities across the province will be tabled at the city’s general committee meeting tomorrow morning. S. as well. In his report, Mississauga’s Planning and Building Commissioner Andrew Whittemore notes the provincial government on Aug. ” Two weeks earlier, city councillors unanimously agreed to impose a moratorium of one year — and up to two years — on data centre developments in Mississauga to allow the city more time to study the matter and any new rules that would regulate the rapidly growing industry. Council’s decision followed some two dozen deputations from residents and other stakeholders at the July 29 city council meeting, the vast majority of whom spoke against the large new facilities. ” He added “significant regulatory and legislative changes would be needed to implement elements” of the strategy.

items.title: Attendance part of new grading system for Mississauga, Brampton, Caledon students
items.summary: Students across Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon head back to class today, but for high school students especially, it won’t be business as usual. A major change coming to classrooms across Ontario this year will make attendance and participation part of students’ final grades, while most secondary students will also face mandatory final evaluations, including written exams. The new rules apply to students in Grades 9 to 12 and are being implemented by both the Peel District School Board (PDSB) and the Dufferin-Peel Catholic District School Board (DPCDSB). Under the new provincial assessment rules, students in Grades 9 and 10 will have their final marks calculated using three components: 65 per cent for classroom work, 20 per cent for mandatory final evaluations and 15 per cent for attendance and participation. For students in Grades 11 and 12, classroom work will account for 65 per cent, mandatory final evaluations 25 per cent and attendance and participation 10 per cent. That means showing up and taking part in class can now directly affect a student’s final mark. The province says excused absences, including illness, unavoidable circumstances, inclement weather and approved cultural or religious observances, will not negatively affect a student’s grade. The final-evaluation requirement is also changing how secondary students will finish their courses.

items.title: New Indigenous market a first for Mississauga mall
items.summary: The owner of a new Indigenous market in a Mississauga mall went from struggles with addiction to running a successful business. BigCanoe Indigenous Market will open at Erin Mills Town Centre during National Truth and Reconciliation Month. It is the first Indigenous-owned and operated storefront in a Mississauga mall. A family business, owned and operated by Jared BigCanoe, the vision is to continue a family legacy by creating an authentic space to engage in Indigenous traditions through storytelling, ceremony, healing, art, beading and trading culturally crafted handmade Indigenous goods. Jared, a member of the Georgina Island First Nation, experienced intergenerational trauma. His grandmother and grandfather attended the Spanish Residential School in northern Ontario. Residential Schools were government-funded, church-run institutions that operated across Canada for over a century. Their purpose was to assimilate First Nations children by forcibly separating them from their families, languages, and cultures. Though these schools are now closed, their effects continue to be deeply felt. The BigCanoe family experienced confinement, loss of culture, loss of heritage, severe economic restrictions, dehumanization and loss of family. com. ” “I was pretty much homeless, and I was experiencing some troubles with opiate addiction,” he said.

items.title: Fourteen Candidates Register for Mississauga's October Mayoral Race
items.summary: According to CityNews Toronto, a total of 14 candidates have registered to run for mayor of Mississauga in the city's October 26 municipal election. The outlet reports incumbent Mayor Carolyn Parrish, who won the seat in a 2024 byelection after decades as a city councillor and federal Liberal MP, is seeking to hold onto the position. CityNews Toronto reports polling from Liaison Strategies published August 14 suggests the race has narrowed to a head-to-head contest between Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie. According to the outlet, Crombie served a decade as Mississauga's mayor before resigning in 2024 to lead the Ontario Liberal Party, then stepped down from that role after failing to win a seat in the 2025 provincial election. CityNews Toronto reports Crombie is now looking to return to her former job in what is expected to be a high-stakes race.

items.title: A decade of winning: Mississauga is a ‘top performer’ in Canada, attracting business and investment
items.summary: Site Selection Magazine names Mississauga one of Canada’s best locations for business and investment for the 10th year in a row. Mississauga has once again been recognized as one of Canada’s leading locations for business investment and expansion, earning a spot on Site Selection Magazine’s list of top-performing Canadian communities for the 10th consecutive year. The publication described Mississauga as a “perennial top performer,” highlighting the City’s ability to attract investment, support business growth and create jobs. 7 billion in corporate investment, according to Site Selection’s award details. The recognition reflects the strength of Mississauga’s diverse economy and its continued appeal to investors in sectors including advanced manufacturing, logistics, life sciences, technology and financial services. Key events and achievements contributed to the award. Invest Mississauga continued to attract new business opportunities through international outreach and business development initiatives, including a Global Affairs Canada-led mission to Zurich and London. The team also led sector-focused business engagement with life sciences, advanced manufacturing and technology industry leaders in Canada and key international markets. Invest Mississauga welcomed the City’s film, television and music production office into its portfolio and helped advance the local creative economy. In addition, Council made the City’s live music grant program permanent, strengthening support for the cultural sector. IDEA Mississauga, Invest Mississauga’s entrepreneurship hub, continued to support innovation and business growth and job creation throughout 2024-25. Companies participating in IDEA programs raised more than $15 million in funding, generated $4 million in annual revenue and created 270 local jobs. The hub also welcomed a delegation of Japanese technology companies, strengthening international business connections and investment opportunities.
